title: Trump Administration Proposes Permanent $103,265 H-1B Fee in New Regulation
excerpt: DHS publishes proposed rule in the Federal Register to codify the controversial visa charge struck down by courts, with a 30-day public comment period beginning Tuesday.
body:
• DHS proposed a $103,265 fee on new H-1B visas, published in the Federal Register on Monday with a 30-day comment period.
  • The regulation aims to make permanent a fee Trump first imposed via proclamation in September 2025, which courts blocked as an unlawful tax.
  • H-1B registrations have already dropped more than 25% since 2024; the fee could further discourage employer sponsorship.
  • Multiple lawsuits challenging the fee are still pending in federal courts; the new regulation could face fresh legal challenges.

The Trump administration on Monday released a proposed regulation to permanently codify a more than $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers — a charge that federal courts have blocked but the administration has refused to abandon.

The Department of Homeland Security posted the proposed $103,265 fee in the Federal Register on Monday, with formal publication set for Tuesday. The filing opens a 30-day public comment period, and the rule could be finalized by the end of the year, according to Reuters.

From Proclamation to Permanent Rule

Trump first imposed the $100,000 H-1B fee through a presidential proclamation in September 2025, invoking his authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry of foreign nationals deemed detrimental to U.S. interests. That proclamation — which expires one year after issuance in September 2026 — directed DHS to adopt regulations making the fee permanent.

The fee has faced fierce legal opposition. A federal judge in Boston ruled in June that the charge constituted an unlawful tax that Congress never authorized and blocked the administration from collecting it. A Boston-based appeals court is currently reviewing that decision, while a separate court considers whether a Washington, D.C. judge properly rejected a challenge brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court, Boston

Industry Impact and Declining Applications

The fee represents a dramatic escalation in the cost of sponsoring H-1B workers. Employers previously paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in fees depending on company size and other factors. The proposed charge would multiply that cost by roughly 20 times.

The chilling effect is already measurable. As of late February, only about 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications, according to court filings. H-1B registrations fell to about 344,000 last year, down more than 25% from 2024 and less than half the 794,000 sought in 2023, according to USCIS data.

The fee hits hardest in industries that rely heavily on H-1B workers, including technology, education, healthcare, and academic research. Business groups have argued the program is essential to fill roles where qualified American workers are unavailable.

Legal Challenges Multiply

The proposed regulation arrives amid a thicket of pending lawsuits. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Democratic-led states, and a coalition of unions and employers have all filed legal challenges against the fee. Those cases could be amended to target the newly proposed rule once finalized.

Opponents argue that the president's power to restrict entry does not extend to overriding the statute that created the H-1B program, and that DHS cannot impose fees or taxes to generate revenue without Congressional authorization. The administration maintains the fee is not a traditional tax and that courts have limited standing to question presidential authority over immigration.

What It Means for Indian Workers

Indian nationals have historically been the largest group of H-1B recipients, and the fee has generated significant anxiety among Indian tech workers and students planning to enter the U.S. workforce. The proposed regulation comes on top of a separate DHS rule earlier this month that added fees of up to $4,500 for H-1B extension and transfer petitions.

The administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would prioritize higher-skilled, better-paid workers — a shift that could further reshape which Indian workers gain access to the program.

What's Next

The 30-day public comment period begins with Tuesday's formal publication. Industry groups, advocacy organizations, and individual stakeholders can submit comments challenging or supporting the proposed rule. Once the comment period closes, DHS will review submissions before issuing a final regulation. Given the pace of the rulemaking, the fee could be formalized into law by the end of 2026, though ongoing court battles could delay or block implementation.
